axiom_nodes.title: I AM: The Root Speaks — Full Draft
axiom_nodes.summary: This paper argues that Christianity is grounded not merely in upward inference from world to God but in God's self-disclosure, paradigmatically in the divine name 'I AM WHO I AM' (Exodus 3:14) and in Jesus' first-person 'I am' identity claims in John's Gospel. It distinguishes discovery (what the world requires) from disclosure (who God says He is), insists they converge without collapsing, and frames the disclosed portrait as statable before it is proven. It maps most directly onto the axiom system's self-grounding, self-existence, and revelation/Logos nodes, with secondary resonance to observer/terminal-observer and information-primacy themes.

axiom_nodes.name: A2.2 — Self-Grounding
axiom_nodes.evidence_quote: If something deeper explains God, then God was not the root.
axiom_nodes.notes: The paper's central claim that God is not defined by anything beneath or larger than Himself directly asserts self-grounding.

axiom_nodes.name: A1.1 — Existence
axiom_nodes.evidence_quote: He is the One from whom every “is” receives its existence.
axiom_nodes.notes: God as source of all existence, named from His own existence ('I AM').

axiom_nodes.name: A2.1 — Substrate Requirement
axiom_nodes.evidence_quote: You cannot place God inside a category larger than God, because then the category would be more ultimate than God.
axiom_nodes.notes: Argues against any deeper substrate explaining God; supports the requirement that the ultimate root be substrate, not dependent.

axiom_nodes.name: A1.2 — Distinction
axiom_nodes.evidence_quote: If God is personal, and if creation is not God, then creatures should not assume that their upward reasoning is the only possible route to knowledge of Him.
axiom_nodes.notes: Creator/creature distinction is assumed and used to ground the possibility of revelation.

axiom_nodes.name: A5.1 — Observation Requirement
axiom_nodes.evidence_quote: We can look at existence, truth, relation, order, consciousness, morality, beauty, suffering, and history.
axiom_nodes.notes: The paper treats creaturely observation/reasoning as a real route (discovery) but does not assert the axiom that observation is metaphysically required.

axiom_nodes.name: BC1 — Terminal Observer Exists
axiom_nodes.evidence_quote: God is not first introduced as an object lying on a table, waiting for creatures to define Him.
axiom_nodes.notes: God as the self-naming, self-disclosing One who is not an object within the system resonates with the terminal observer role, though the paper does not use that vocabulary.

axiom_nodes.name: ID7.1 — Terminal Observer Is God
axiom_nodes.evidence_quote: It says the Root entered history and spoke in the first person.
axiom_nodes.notes: The identification of the root/Logos with the God who speaks and enters history in Christ supports the terminal-observer-is-God identification.

axiom_nodes.name: LAMBDA - Logos Christ Completion
axiom_nodes.evidence_quote: It says the Root entered history and spoke in the first person.
axiom_nodes.notes: Christ as the personal self-disclosure of the root is the paper's central Christological claim.

axiom_nodes.name: PERSONHOOD — Agency, Intentionality, Relational Capacity
axiom_nodes.evidence_quote: He is the One who calls, commands, creates, names, promises, judges, forgives, and reveals.
axiom_nodes.notes: God is explicitly described with agency, intentionality, and relational capacity.

axiom_nodes.name: A1.3 — Information Primacy
axiom_nodes.evidence_quote: Christianity does not merely say Jesus brought information about the root.
axiom_nodes.notes: The paper distinguishes information-about from identity-disclosure but does not assert information as ontologically primitive.

axiom_nodes.name: BC2 — Grace External To System
axiom_nodes.evidence_quote: But if God has spoken, then the highest form of knowledge is not guessing correctly about a silent source.
axiom_nodes.notes: God's self-disclosure comes from outside creaturely reach, structurally parallel to grace as external intervention, though grace is not the paper's term.

axiom_nodes.name: BC8 — Voluntary Coupling
axiom_nodes.evidence_quote: A skeptic does not have to accept the Bible’s authority to understand what this paper is doing.
axiom_nodes.notes: The paper preserves the reader's freedom to withhold assent, but does not develop voluntary coupling as an axiom.

axiom_nodes.name: A9.1 — External Intervention Required
axiom_nodes.evidence_quote: But Christianity is not built only on upward inference.
axiom_nodes.notes: Argues that creaturely inference is insufficient and external divine disclosure is required.

axiom_nodes.name: A7.1 — Closure Requirement
axiom_nodes.evidence_quote: The investigation happens where those two meet.
axiom_nodes.notes: The convergence of reason and revelation gestures toward closure but the paper does not assert a formal closure requirement.

axiom_nodes.name: A7.2 — Uniqueness From Boundary Conditions
axiom_nodes.notes: Mentions comparing rival answers but does not develop uniqueness-from-boundary-conditions.

axiom_nodes.name: T16.1 — Christianity 8 of 8 BCs
axiom_nodes.evidence_quote: The support layer must face the historical questions, the Johannine context, rival religious claims, translation issues, and resurrection evidence.
axiom_nodes.notes: Acknowledges rival religious claims and the need for support-layer work but does not assert the 8-of-8 BC claim.

axiom_nodes.name: BRIDGE-PHY-THEO - Physics-Theology Bridge
axiom_nodes.notes: The paper explicitly frames science, philosophy, and Scripture as convergent but distinct methods, which is the bridge posture.

atoms.title: I AM: The Root Speaks — Full Draft
atoms.summary: This paper argues that if God is the ultimate root of reality, the central question is not merely whether humans can reason upward to Him, but whether He has spoken. It presents the biblical claim that God discloses Himself—naming Himself 'I AM WHO I AM' to Moses, and in Christ taking that divine identity into history. The paper distinguishes discovery (what the world requires) from disclosure (whom God says He is), and argues that Christianity is built not only on inference but on God's self-revelation, which must be received rather than merely deduced.

atoms.name: The Root Speaks
atoms.statementTechnical: Christianity does not merely claim that God can be inferred; it claims that God has disclosed Himself.
atoms.statementPlain: Christianity says God has actually spoken and shown us who He is, not just that we can figure Him out by reasoning.
atoms.falsificationCondition: If Christianity's authoritative texts and central tradition did not claim divine self-disclosure, or if the claim that God has spoken were shown to be a later invention with no basis in the earliest Christian movement, this claim would be falsified.
atoms.notes: This is the central claim of the paper, stated in the [!claim] callout at P79.

atoms.name: The Divine Name as Boundary
atoms.statementTechnical: The name 'I AM WHO I AM' (Exodus 3:14) functions as a boundary that prevents God from being defined by anything more ultimate than Himself; it names God from the side of His own self-existent existence.
atoms.statementPlain: When God says 'I AM WHO I AM,' He is not giving a label like other names. He is saying He cannot be defined by anything deeper or larger—He is the root, not a thing among things.
atoms.falsificationCondition: If Exodus 3:14 could be shown to be a creaturely label that places God within a larger category, or if the text's grammar and context clearly indicate God is being named by comparison to other beings, this claim would be falsified.
atoms.notes: Based on Exodus 3:14 and the surrounding argument in P12–P26.

atoms.name: Jesus Takes the Divine Name
atoms.statementTechnical: In John's Gospel, Jesus applies the 'I am' formula to Himself with predicates that identify Him with the divine root, not merely as a teacher or prophet.
atoms.statementPlain: Jesus doesn't just talk about God—He says things like 'I am the bread of life' and 'I am the truth,' using the same 'I am' language God used for Himself. That's identity language, not just religious advice.
atoms.falsificationCondition: If the Johannine 'I am' sayings could be shown to be later theological additions with no historical connection to Jesus, or if they functioned merely as ordinary metaphors without identity claims, this claim would be falsified.
atoms.notes: Based on the list of 'I am' sayings in John's Gospel (P42–P53).

atoms.name: Disclosure and Discovery Are Distinct but Convergent
atoms.statementTechnical: Discovery asks what the world requires; disclosure asks whom God says He is. These are distinct epistemic routes that should converge without being collapsed into one method.
atoms.statementPlain: We can study the world to learn about God (discovery), and we can listen to what God says about Himself (disclosure). They are different, but they should fit together.
atoms.falsificationCondition: If discovery and disclosure were shown to be mutually exclusive or contradictory, or if one method consistently yielded results incompatible with the other, this claim would be falsified.
atoms.notes: Stated in the [!bridge] callout at P38 and developed in P28–P37.

atoms.name: Christianity Is Built on Disclosure, Not Only Inference
atoms.statementTechnical: Christianity is not built only on upward inference from effects to cause; it is built on God's self-disclosure in speech, action, covenant, and ultimately in Christ.
atoms.statementPlain: Christianity doesn't just rely on arguments from the world to God. It relies on God actually speaking, acting, making promises, and coming into history.
atoms.falsificationCondition: If Christianity's foundational documents and earliest traditions did not center on divine self-disclosure but only on human inference, or if the disclosure events (e.g., Exodus, Incarnation) were shown to be unhistorical, this claim would be falsified.

atoms.name: The Disclosed Portrait Can Be Stated Before It Is Proven
atoms.statementTechnical: The Christian portrait of God—self-existent, non-derived, personal, speaking, faithful, and revealed in Christ—can be stated honestly as a claim before it is publicly proven, and then tested for convergence with reality, reason, history, and experience.
atoms.statementPlain: We can describe what Christianity says about God without first proving it. Then we can ask whether the world, our reasoning, history, and our experience line up with that description.
atoms.falsificationCondition: If the disclosed portrait were incoherent or could not be stated without presupposing its own truth, or if no possible convergence test could be formulated, this claim would be falsified.

atoms.name: Disclosure and Discovery Bridge
atoms.statementTechnical: Discovery asks what the world requires; disclosure asks whom God says He is.
atoms.statementPlain: Discovery is about what the world needs to be explained; disclosure is about who God says He is.

atoms.name: Exodus 3:14 — I AM WHO I AM
atoms.statementTechnical: Exodus 3:14 records God's self-naming to Moses as 'I AM WHO I AM.'
atoms.statementPlain: In Exodus 3:14, God tells Moses His name is 'I AM WHO I AM.'
atoms.notes: Scripture citation used as evidence for the claim about the divine name.

atoms.name: Johannine 'I Am' Sayings
atoms.statementTechnical: The Gospel of John records Jesus using 'I am' with predicates such as bread of life, light of the world, door, good shepherd, resurrection and life, way/truth/life, and true vine.
atoms.statementPlain: In John's Gospel, Jesus says things like 'I am the bread of life' and 'I am the way, the truth, and the life.'

atoms.name: The Skeptic's Objection
atoms.statementTechnical: A skeptic does not have to accept the Bible's authority to understand the paper's project; the paper is not arguing 'Exodus 3:14 is in the Bible, therefore God exists.'
atoms.statementPlain: You don't have to believe the Bible to follow what this paper is saying. It's not saying 'the Bible says it, so it's true.'

atoms.name: Revelation Can Be Misunderstood or False
atoms.statementTechnical: Revelation can be misunderstood, claims of revelation can be false, Scripture must be interpreted, history must be investigated, and the Church can mishandle what it receives.
atoms.statementPlain: People can misunderstand revelation, false claims of revelation exist, the Bible needs interpretation, history needs checking, and the Church can get it wrong.

atoms.name: Convergence of Reason and Revelation
atoms.statementTechnical: If Christianity is true, reality, reason, history, and experience will converge with the disclosed portrait of God.
atoms.statementPlain: If Christianity is true, then what we find in the world, in logic, in history, and in our lives should fit with the God it describes.

atoms.name: Has God Spoken?
atoms.statementTechnical: If God is the root, the first problem is not only whether we can reach Him, but whether He has spoken.
atoms.statementPlain: If God is the ultimate source, the big question isn't just whether we can find Him—it's whether He has spoken.
atoms.notes: Opening question of the paper, P02–P03.

atoms.name: The Child and the Father Analogy
atoms.statementTechnical: A child can learn about his father by studying the house the father built or by hearing the father speak; these are not enemies.
atoms.statementPlain: A kid can learn about his dad by looking at the house he built or by listening to him talk. Both are valid.
atoms.notes: Analogy in P30–P34, used to illustrate discovery and disclosure.

source_selection.exact_source_expression: When God says 'I AM WHO I AM,' He is not giving a label like other names. He is saying He cannot be defined by anything deeper or larger—He is the root, not a thing among things.
source_selection.reason: The claim has a clear logical structure: a self-naming entity that is not definable by anything deeper or larger, i.e., not a member of a larger category and not explained by a more fundamental entity. This can be modeled as a partial order of metaphysical dependence with a maximal element.

formal_object.exact_proposed_statement: A root is an entity r such that there is no entity x with x < r in the dependence order, and r is not a member of any category C that is more fundamental than r.

symbol_table.reader_meaning: Any being or thing that can stand in dependence relations.
x depends on y if y is deeper, larger, or more fundamental than x.
An entity that is not dependent on anything deeper and is not a member of a more fundamental category.

explicit_premises: DependsOn is a strict partial order (irreflexive, transitive, asymmetric).
There exists at least one Entity.
assumptions_and_dependencies.theological_starting_premises: The biblical claim that God is the root and not a thing among things.
assumptions_and_dependencies.non_vacuity_requirement: There must exist at least one entity satisfying Root, or the definition is vacuously true but not instantiated.

verification_controls.interpretation: Lean corpus was not searched; no compilation attempted.
No proof of existence of a Root entity.

result_and_boundary.what_is_established: A formal definition of a root entity in a dependence order.
result_and_boundary.what_remains_open: Whether any entity satisfies this definition; whether the dependence order is well-founded; whether the biblical God is the unique root.
result_and_boundary.encoding_fidelity_review: The formalization captures the negative claim (not defined by anything deeper or larger) but does not capture the positive claim of self-existence or the personal nature of God.
result_and_boundary.interpretive_connections: Connects to classical theism's concept of God as ultimate ground of being.

source_selection.exact_source_expression: We can study the world to learn about God (discovery), and we can listen to what God says about Himself (disclosure). They are different, but they should fit together.
source_selection.reason: The claim asserts a compatibility relation between two distinct epistemic sources: discovery (reason from world) and disclosure (revelation). This can be modeled as two sets of propositions that are consistent.

formal_object.exact_proposed_statement: If Discovery and Disclosure are sets of propositions, and both are true, then their union is consistent.

symbol_table.reader_meaning: Propositions about God derived from studying the world.
Propositions about God derived from God's self-revelation.
No contradiction can be derived from the set.

explicit_premises: Discovery and Disclosure are sets of propositions.
Both Discovery and Disclosure are true (i.e., all their members are true).
assumptions_and_dependencies.theological_starting_premises: If Christianity is true, then what we find in the world and what God says should fit together.
assumptions_and_dependencies.non_vacuity_requirement: Discovery and Disclosure must be non-empty for the theorem to be meaningful.

verification_controls.interpretation: Lean corpus was not searched; no compilation attempted.
No proof that Discovery and Disclosure are non-empty.

result_and_boundary.what_is_established: A formal statement of the convergence claim: if both sources are true, they are consistent.
result_and_boundary.what_remains_open: Whether Discovery and Disclosure are in fact true and non-empty; whether the consistency is provable without assuming the conclusion.
result_and_boundary.encoding_fidelity_review: The formalization captures the logical compatibility but not the epistemic process of how they converge.
result_and_boundary.interpretive_connections: Relates to natural theology and revealed theology debates.

source_selection.exact_source_expression: Jesus doesn't just talk about God—He says things like 'I am the bread of life' and 'I am the truth,' using the same 'I am' language God used for Himself. That's identity language, not just religious advice.
source_selection.reason: The claim is about identity statements: Jesus uses 'I am' predicates that ascribe to Himself properties that are divine or ultimate. This can be modeled as a set of identity claims and a relation of 'divine predicate'.

formal_object.exact_proposed_statement: A divine identity claim is a statement of the form 'Jesus is P' where P is a predicate that is also used of God in the Hebrew Bible or is a role that only God can fulfill.

symbol_table.reader_meaning: The historical person Jesus of Nazareth.
A property that is uniquely divine or ultimate.
A statement where Jesus predicates a divine property of Himself.

explicit_premises: There is a set of predicates considered divine.
Jesus utters statements of the form 'I am P' where P is divine.
assumptions_and_dependencies.theological_starting_premises: The New Testament records Jesus using 'I am' sayings.
assumptions_and_dependencies.non_vacuity_requirement: There must be at least one divine predicate and one such utterance by Jesus.

verification_controls.interpretation: Lean corpus was not searched; no compilation attempted.
No proof that such predicates exist or that Jesus uttered them.

result_and_boundary.what_is_established: A formal definition of divine identity claims.
result_and_boundary.what_remains_open: Whether the historical Jesus actually made these claims; whether the predicates are truly divine; whether the 'I am' sayings are correctly translated.
result_and_boundary.encoding_fidelity_review: The formalization captures the logical form but not the theological interpretation of the sayings.
result_and_boundary.interpretive_connections: Connects to Christology and the study of the historical Jesus.

source_selection.exact_source_expression: If Christianity is true, then what we find in the world, in logic, in history, and in our lives should fit with the God it describes.
source_selection.reason: This is a conditional prediction: if Christianity is true, then there is a fit between the world and the Christian description of God. This can be modeled as a consistency condition between a set of observations and a set of theological claims.

formal_object.exact_proposed_statement: If Christianity is true, then for every observation O in the set of observations, O is consistent with the Christian description of God.

symbol_table.reader_meaning: The truth of the Christian worldview.
Propositions about the world, logic, history, and experience.
Propositions describing God according to Christianity.
The union of the two sets is consistent.

assumptions_and_dependencies.theological_starting_premises: The Christian claim that God is the root and has disclosed Himself.
assumptions_and_dependencies.non_vacuity_requirement: Observation and ChristianDescription must be non-empty.

verification_controls.interpretation: Lean corpus was not searched; no compilation attempted.

result_and_boundary.what_is_established: A formal conditional statement of the convergence prediction.
result_and_boundary.what_remains_open: Whether Christianity is true; whether the observations actually fit; whether the consistency can be proven without assuming Christianity.
result_and_boundary.encoding_fidelity_review: The formalization captures the logical form but not the evidential weight of the convergence.
result_and_boundary.interpretive_connections: Relates to apologetics and the problem of divine hiddenness.

source_selection.exact_source_expression: We can describe what Christianity says about God without first proving it. Then we can ask whether the world, our reasoning, history, and our experience line up with that description.
source_selection.reason: This is a methodological claim: the disclosed portrait can be stated as a set of propositions without proof, and then evaluated for consistency with other data. This can be modeled as a separation between statement and verification.

formal_object.exact_proposed_statement: A disclosed portrait is a set of propositions about God that can be stated without proof and later evaluated for consistency with observations.

symbol_table.reader_meaning: The set of claims Christianity makes about God.
The set can be formulated without requiring a proof of its truth.
The portrait is checked against observations for consistency.

explicit_premises: There is a set of propositions describing God according to Christianity.
There is a set of observations from world, reason, history, and experience.
assumptions_and_dependencies.theological_starting_premises: The Christian claim that God has disclosed Himself.
assumptions_and_dependencies.non_vacuity_requirement: The disclosed portrait must be non-empty.

verification_controls.interpretation: Lean corpus was not searched; no compilation attempted.
No proof that the portrait is non-empty or that consistency holds.

result_and_boundary.what_remains_open: Whether the portrait is true; whether the observations actually line up; whether the method is sound.
result_and_boundary.encoding_fidelity_review: The formalization captures the methodological separation but not the content of the portrait.

stories.title_or_label: The Child and the Father Analogy
stories.setting_or_context: A child learning about his father through two routes: studying the house the father built and hearing the father speak.
stories.plot_or_sequence: A child can study the house the father built—its order, rooms, table, locks, tools, boundaries, repairs, signs of care. The child can also hear the father speak. These are not enemies: the house witnesses to the father, and the father's voice explains the house. This maps onto science studying the house, philosophy asking what the house requires, Scripture recording the Father speaking, and Christ revealing the Father personally.
stories.emotional_or_rhetorical_load: Warm, domestic, intuitive; lowers the stakes of the disclosure/discovery distinction by making it feel like ordinary family life rather than a methodological crisis.

boundaries.what_it_shows: That two distinct routes to knowledge of a person—inference from artifacts and direct speech—can coexist and converge without collapsing into one method.
boundaries.what_it_does_not_show: That the father actually exists, that the house actually has a builder, that the father has actually spoken, or that any particular claim of divine speech is true. It also does not show that the two routes will in fact converge in any given case.
boundaries.what_would_falsify_the_narrative: If the two routes were shown to be mutually exclusive or systematically contradictory—e.g., if listening to the father reliably contradicted what the house revealed—the analogy's convergence claim would fail.

stories.notes: The analogy is illustrative and motivational; it carries no independent evidential weight for the existence or speech of God. It is structurally load-bearing for the paper's posture (A07) but not for its truth.

stories.title_or_label: Moses at the Burning Bush: The Divine Name as Boundary
stories.setting_or_context: Moses asks God for His name; God answers from the burning bush with 'I AM WHO I AM.'
stories.plot_or_sequence: God is introduced not as an object awaiting definition but as the One who calls, commands, creates, names, promises, judges, forgives, and reveals. When Moses asks for His name, God does not give a creaturely label but says 'I AM WHO I AM.' This is not a slogan but a boundary: God is not one being inside a larger field of being, not a powerful object in the universe, not the biggest thing among things. He is the One from whom every 'is' receives its existence. The name refuses to let God be measured from below; it names Him from His own side. It does not answer every philosophical question or remove mystery, but it tells us where not to look: not as one more dependent thing, not downstream.
stories.emotional_or_rhetorical_load: Reverent, awe-inducing, boundary-setting; the narrative carries the weight of a foundational self-disclosure that reorients the entire investigation.

boundaries.what_it_shows: The shape of the biblical claim about God's self-naming: that the divine name functions as a boundary against treating God as a dependent being among beings.
boundaries.what_it_does_not_show: That the Exodus narrative is historically accurate, that God actually spoke to Moses, or that the metaphysical reading of the name is the only or correct interpretation. It also does not prove that God exists or that the biblical text is authoritative.
boundaries.what_would_falsify_the_narrative: Historical or textual evidence that Exodus 3:14 is a late composition with no connection to Moses, or that the Hebrew 'ehyeh asher ehyeh' is better read as a creaturely label or a refusal to give a name rather than a self-designation of underived existence.

stories.notes: This narrative is structurally load-bearing: the paper's central claim (A01, A02) depends on the reading of Exodus 3:14. The historical content is flagged as evidence atom A08 but is not independently verified in this paper; the support layer is said to face historical questions (S091).

stories.title_or_label: Jesus Takes the Divine Name: The Johannine 'I Am' Sayings
stories.source_span: [P39]–[P57], S068–S094; John's Gospel cited at [P43] S072–S078
stories.setting_or_context: In John's Gospel, Jesus repeatedly uses 'I am' language and attaches to Himself roles too large for a mere teacher.
stories.plot_or_sequence: Jesus does not merely speak about God from a distance; He identifies Himself in ways that press the root question into history. He says 'I am the bread of life,' 'I am the light of the world,' 'I am the door,' 'I am the good shepherd,' 'I am the resurrection and the life,' 'I am the way, and the truth, and the life,' 'I am the true vine.' A prophet can say 'God gives bread'; Jesus says 'I am the bread.' A teacher can say 'I will show you truth'; Jesus says 'I am the truth.' A guide can say 'I know the way'; Jesus says 'I am the way.' A comforter can say 'God will raise the dead'; Jesus says 'I am the resurrection and the life.' This is identity language, not ordinary religious advice. It does not prove by itself that Jesus is who Christianity says He is—anyone can make a large claim—but the shape of the claim is unmistakable: Christianity says the Root entered history and spoke in the first person.
stories.emotional_or_rhetorical_load: High, dramatic, almost confrontational; the repeated contrast between what a prophet/teacher/guide/ comforter says and what Jesus says builds a rhetorical crescendo around identity rather than advice.

boundaries.what_it_shows: The rhetorical shape and identity-claim structure of the Johannine 'I am' sayings, and how they differ from ordinary prophetic or teaching speech.
boundaries.what_it_does_not_show: That Jesus actually said these things, that the Johannine sayings are historically reliable, that they are correctly translated or interpreted as claims to divinity, or that Jesus is in fact divine. The paper explicitly concedes this (S089–S091).
boundaries.what_would_falsify_the_narrative: Evidence that the Johannine 'I am' sayings are late theological constructions with no historical basis in Jesus' own speech, or that the Greek 'egō eimi' in these passages is not intended as a divine-name claim.

stories.notes: Structurally load-bearing for the paper's christological claim (A03). The paper itself flags that the support layer must face historical questions, Johannine context, rival claims, translation issues, and resurrection evidence (S091).

stories.title_or_label: The Skeptic's Objection and the Disclosed Portrait
stories.setting_or_context: A rhetorical framing in which a skeptic is addressed directly and assured that belief in the Bible's authority is not required to follow the paper's argument.
stories.plot_or_sequence: A skeptic does not have to accept the Bible's authority to understand what the paper is doing. The paper is not saying 'Exodus 3:14 is in the Bible, therefore God exists.' It is saying: 'If Christianity is being treated as testimony, this is the kind of God it identifies: self-existent, non-derived, personal, speaking, faithful, and finally revealed in Christ.' That is a different claim. The disclosed portrait can be stated honestly before it is proven publicly. We can ask what Christianity claims, then ask whether reality, reason, history, and experience converge with that claim. The public story needs both movements: reason climbs, God speaks, and the investigation happens where those two meet.
stories.emotional_or_rhetorical_load: Conciliatory, disarming, invitational; it lowers the barrier for skeptical readers by distinguishing the paper's descriptive task from a proof of God's existence.

boundaries.what_it_shows: That the paper's method is to state the Christian disclosure-claim descriptively before arguing for it, and that this method does not require the reader to grant biblical authority at the outset.
boundaries.what_it_does_not_show: That the disclosed portrait is true, that reality/reason/history/experience actually converge with it, or that the convergence argument succeeds. It only shows the structure of the proposed investigation.
boundaries.what_would_falsify_the_narrative: If the paper were shown to actually depend on biblical authority for its descriptive claim, or if the convergence test were shown to be unfalsifiable or vacuous, the distinction between 'stating the portrait' and 'proving it' would collapse.

stories.notes: This is a meta-rhetorical arc about the paper's own method rather than a story about events. It is separable from the substantive argument but shapes how the argument is received.

stories.title_or_label: The Root Speaks: The Central Sermon Arc
stories.setting_or_context: The paper's overarching framing: if God is the root, the first problem is not only whether we can reach Him but whether He has spoken.
stories.plot_or_sequence: Human beings can reason upward—looking at existence, truth, relation, order, consciousness, morality, beauty, suffering, and history—and ask what kind of root could carry all of that. But if God is actually God, He is not trapped at the far end of our investigation. The root can disclose Himself. That is the biblical claim. If God remains only an inference, every argument about God stays trapped inside creaturely reach. But Christianity is not built only on upward inference; it is built on disclosure. God speaks, acts, covenants, comes, names Himself, reveals His character, and enters the human story in Christ. This does not remove the need for argument—revelation can be misunderstood, claims of revelation can be false, Scripture must be interpreted, history investigated, the Church can mishandle what it receives—but if God has spoken, the highest form of knowledge is not guessing correctly about a silent source; it is receiving the One who gives Himself to be known. The root is not silent. The root speaks. And in Christ, Christianity says, the root walks into the room.
stories.emotional_or_rhetorical_load: Elevated, declarative, almost homiletic; the closing lines ('the root walks into the room') are designed to land with emotional and rhetorical force.

boundaries.what_it_shows: The overall shape of the paper's thesis: that Christianity claims divine disclosure, not merely human inference, and that this reframes the entire investigation.
boundaries.what_it_does_not_show: That God has in fact spoken, that Christianity is true, that the convergence of reason and revelation obtains, or that the biblical texts are reliable. The paper explicitly acknowledges that revelation can be misunderstood and false claims exist (S112–S116).
boundaries.what_would_falsify_the_narrative: If it were shown that no credible instance of divine disclosure exists, or that the Christian claim reduces entirely to human inference, the sermon arc's central contrast would collapse.

stories.notes: This is the paper's master narrative frame; it is not separable from the argument because the argument's entire structure is built around the disclosure/discovery distinction it dramatizes.

narrative_arc.opening_device: A conditional premise: 'If God is the root, then the first problem is not only whether we can reach Him. It is whether He has spoken.' This reframes the usual apologetic question from human ascent to divine initiative.
narrative_arc.central_tension: The tension between discovery (human reasoning upward from the world) and disclosure (God speaking from His own side). The paper argues that Christianity is built on the latter, not merely the former, while insisting the two must converge rather than collapse into one method.
narrative_arc.resolution_or_payoff: The resolution is the claim that the root is not silent—God speaks, acts, covenants, comes, names Himself, and enters history in Christ. The payoff is the closing image: 'the root walks into the room.'

stories.notes: The paper is heavily narrative and homiletic in structure. Its stories function primarily as explanatory and motivational devices; none of them independently establish the truth of the claims they illustrate. The Exodus and Johannine narratives are the most structurally load-bearing, and the paper itself flags that their historical verification belongs to a separate support layer (S091). The child/father analogy is the most clearly separable illustration. The skeptic-facing arc is a meta-rhetorical frame about method rather than a story about events.

core_relation.sentence: Christianity is built on God's self-disclosure, not merely on human upward inference; if God has not spoken, the whole claim collapses.

master_equation.one_line: The paper's core claim that Christianity rests on God's self-disclosure rather than inference maps analogously onto the master equation, with disclosure playing the role of external negentropy influx and Christ as the local integrator.
breaks: The paper does not treat the slots as a multiplicative product with a formal zero-collapse; it presents disclosure as necessary but does not quantify or formalize the interaction.
G is framed as personal speech rather than an impersonal negentropy flux, so the analogy to external coherence influx is stretched.
Q is weakly present: the paper does not dwell on unresolved superposition; it moves quickly to actualized disclosure.
The paper adds 'revelation can be misunderstood' and 'claims of revelation can be false' as extra factors not captured by the ten slots.

The paper treats upward inference (reason climbing) as genuinely valuable and not zero — 'Those arguments may matter. Some may be strong.' [S098][S099] — which softens the strict multiplicative collapse: reason is not a zero factor, so the product test is closer to 'disclosure is necessary but inference is additive support' than to a pure χ-style product.

The 'child can hear his father speak' analogy [S053] imports a relational/personal factor that has no clean slot in the master equation's factor list; it is closer to a background condition than a multiplicative term.

The paper explicitly disclaims that its claim proves itself: 'It does not prove by itself that Jesus is who Christianity says He is.' [S089] — so the slot mapping describes the shape of the claim, not a demonstrated derivation.
Slot F is stretched: the paper's non-local correlation is theological (Christ as the root entering history) rather than a physical correlation between related systems.
extra_factors: The possibility of false revelation and the need for historical investigation (S113-S115).
The Church's potential mishandling of revelation (S116).
The distinction between disclosure and discovery as two movements (S065-S066).
Historical investigation / resurrection evidence [S091] — treated as a required support layer with no direct master-equation slot.
The distinction between discovery and disclosure [S064][S065][S066] — a methodological factor the equation does not name.
The skeptic's provisional stance [S120][S126] — a rhetorical/epistemic factor that conditions how the claim is received.

overall.summary: The paper maintains a tightly coherent disclosure/discovery framework across its claims, with only minor definitional looseness around 'root' and 'disclosure' and an acknowledged but unresolved evidential gap regarding the Johannine 'I am' sayings.

dimensions.name: internal_consistency
reasons: The central distinction between disclosure and discovery is stated consistently (S047-S049, S064-S066, S129-S132) and never reversed or contradicted.
The claim that revelation does not remove the need for argument (S111-S116) coheres with the earlier concession that the disclosed portrait can be stated before it is proven (S126-S128).
The skeptic-facing clarification (S120-S125) is consistent with the paper's stated posture that it is not arguing 'the Bible says it, so it is true' (S122).

Minor tension: S089-S091 concedes the 'I am' sayings do not prove Jesus' identity and that historical questions remain, yet S092-S094 treats the shape of the claim as 'unmistakable'—this is a rhetorical intensification rather than a logical contradiction, but it slightly strains the paper's otherwise careful epistemic hedging.

dimensions.name: definitional_stability
reasons: 'Disclosure' and 'discovery' are defined functionally and consistently (S064-S066; A04, A07), and the child/father analogy (S050-S056; A14) reinforces the distinction without collapsing it.

'Root' is used throughout as a boundary concept meaning non-derived, non-categorized source (S020-S023, S031-S033, S044-S045), which is stable in use but never given a formal definition—it functions more as a regulative metaphor than a defined term.
'I AM' is characterized as a boundary rather than a label (S018-S019; A02), but the paper does not specify what kind of boundary (semantic, ontological, epistemic), leaving the term underdetermined.

The paper explicitly acknowledges that the name does not answer every philosophical question and does not give a diagram of God's essence (S040-S042), which is a candid admission of definitional limits rather than a defect.

dimensions.name: inferential_connectedness
reasons: The argument moves coherently from the premise that God is root (S002-S003) to the conclusion that disclosure is the primary mode of knowledge (S102-S110), with the bridge atom A07 doing real connective work.
The convergence prediction (A12; S128) is properly framed as a conditional ('If Christianity is true...') rather than an asserted result, which keeps the inference honest.
The paper distinguishes what it is claiming from what it is not claiming (S121-S125), which strengthens inferential clarity.

Gap: the move from 'Jesus uses I am language' (S071-S078) to 'Jesus takes the divine name into Himself' (S068-S070) is asserted rather than argued; the paper acknowledges this needs support (S089-S091) but does not supply the inferential bridge within this text.

dimensions.name: register_boundary_respect
reasons: The paper consistently distinguishes the descriptive/testimonial register from the probative register: it states what Christianity claims (S124) before asking whether reality converges (S127-S128).

The objection handling (S112-S116; A11) explicitly respects the boundary between revelation claims and their verification, listing misunderstanding, false claims, interpretation, history, and ecclesial error as open items.
The skeptic clause (S120-S125; A10) is a model of register discipline: it tells the reader what the paper is not doing before proceeding.
The bridge atom A07 (S064-S066) cleanly separates the two questions ('what the world requires' vs. 'whom God says He is') without conflating them.

tensions.description: The paper asserts that Jesus' 'I am' sayings are identity language pressing the root question into history (S068-S070, S092-S094), while simultaneously conceding that these sayings do not prove the claim and that historical, contextual, and translation questions remain (S089-S091). This is a tension between rhetorical confidence and epistemic caution, not a formal contradiction.

The divine name is said to function as a boundary that refuses measurement from below (S018-S019, S031-S035), yet the paper also invites convergence between disclosure and discovery (S063-S066, S128). If the name is a strict boundary against external definition, the precise sense in which discovery can 'fit' disclosure without measuring it remains under-specified.

missing_definitions.description: Used as a boundary concept for the non-derived source (S020-S023, S031-S033) but never formally defined; its meaning is carried by contrast and metaphor rather than stipulation.
Defined functionally as 'whom God says He is' (S066) but not distinguished from related terms like 'revelation' (S047, S112) or 'testimony' (S124) in a way that fixes its scope.
Applied to the divine name (S019) without specifying whether the boundary is semantic, ontological, or epistemic.

coherence.notes: The paper is unusually self-aware about its own limits: it repeatedly flags what it is not claiming (S121-S125), what remains to be investigated (S089-S091, S112-S116), and where the reader is not required to follow (S120). This self-awareness raises coherence even where definitions remain loose. The main coherence risk is not contradiction but the unargued inferential leap from Johannine 'I am' sayings to identity with the divine name; the paper acknowledges this gap but does not close it within this text. No structural contradictions were found.
